introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Economics 3 (0725), ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2022. Duration: 1 hour 45 minutes.**

INSTRUCTIONS TO CANDIDATES: Answer ANY THREE questions. All questions carry equal marks. You are advised to spend the first fifteen minutes reading the paper. In calculations you are advised to show all the steps in your working. You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers. Calculators are allowed.
enonce_intro_markdown:
The table below presents hypothetical figures of the age distribution of population in two imaginary countries.

| Age Group | Country A (Population '000) | Country B (Population '000) |
|---|---|---|
| 0 - 14 | 50 | 12 |
| 15-64 | 60 | 82 |
| 65+ | 10 | 26 |
incertitudes: Question 2(a) : le sujet ne donne pas la formule du taux de dépendance ; le corrigé retient la définition usuelle (population de 0-14 ans et de 65 ans et plus, divisée par la population de 15-64 ans, en pourcentage), soit 100 % pour le pays A.

Question 2(b) : l'énoncé imprime « (1+4 marks) » ; le corrigé affecte 1 point à la désignation du pays B et 4 points aux raisons. Les chiffres du tableau sont hypothétiques (« imaginary countries ») ; les pourcentages du corrigé en sont calculés (total 120 000 habitants dans chaque pays).
Question 2(d) : les théories sont présentées dans leurs grandes lignes (Malthus, 1798 ; Boserup, 1965) sans citation chiffrée.

Aucun total n'est imprimé par question (« All questions carry equal marks ») : `points` de l'exercice est laissé vide ; les points de chaque sous-question (a), (b)... sont la somme des points imprimés de ses parties ; la somme des points imprimés de chaque question vaut 20.

questions.enonce_markdown: Calculate the dependency ratio for Country A. (4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
The **dependency ratio** compares the **dependants** (those too young or too old to work) with the **working-age population**:

$$\text{Dependency ratio} = \frac{\text{population aged 0-14} + \text{population aged 65 and over}}{\text{population aged 15-64}} \times 100$$

Country A (in thousands): young dependants = 50, old dependants = 10, working-age population = 60.

$$\text{Dependency ratio} = \frac{50 + 10}{60} \times 100 = \frac{60}{60} \times 100 = 100\%$$

The dependency ratio of Country A is **100%** (or 1 : 1): every 100 persons of working age support 100 dependants. Of these, $\frac{50}{60} \times 100 \approx 83.3\%$ are young dependants and $\frac{10}{60} \times 100 \approx 16.7\%$ are old dependants.

questions.enonce_markdown: Which of the two countries is more developed and why? (1+4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Country B** is the more developed (1 mark). Reasons (4 marks), using the table:

| | Country A | Country B |
|---|---|---|
| Total population ('000) | 120 | 120 |
| Aged 0-14 | 50 (41.7%) | 12 (10.0%) |
| Aged 15-64 | 60 (50.0%) | 82 (68.3%) |
| Aged 65+ | 10 (8.3%) | 26 (21.7%) |
| Dependency ratio | 100% | $\frac{12+26}{82}\times 100 \approx 46.3\%$ |

1. **Lower dependency ratio.** B has about 46 dependants per 100 workers against 100 in A, so each worker carries a lighter burden. More income can be saved and invested, which raises output per head.
2. **Larger working population.** Some 68% of B's people are of working age against 50% in A: a bigger labour force relative to total population, and so a higher potential output per head.
3. **Low birth rate.** Only 10% of B's population is under 15 against about 42% in A. A small child population shows low fertility, which is typical of developed countries where families are small, women are educated and incomes are high. A high child share is typical of a developing country with a high birth rate.
4. **High life expectancy.** About 22% of B's population is 65 or over against 8% in A, which suggests good health care, nutrition and living standards.

**Comment:** age structure is only an indicator, since development is measured by income per head, education and health. An ageing population such as B's can also bring heavy pension and health costs, but the data point to B as the more developed.

questions.enonce_markdown: Name three main factors that influence the size of a population. (3 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
The size of a population changes with (1 mark each):

1. **The birth rate** (fertility): the number of live births per 1,000 people per year. A high birth rate increases the population.
2. **The death rate** (mortality): the number of deaths per 1,000 people per year. A fall in the death rate, because of better health care, nutrition and sanitation, raises the population. The difference between births and deaths is the **natural increase**.
3. **Net migration**: immigration minus emigration. Net immigration raises the population, net emigration lowers it.

Other influences, which act through these three, include the age structure, the standard of living, family-planning policy, education of women, wars, epidemics and famine.

questions.enonce_markdown: Briefly explain the major differences between the Malthusian and the Boserup theories of population. (4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Malthusian theory** (Thomas Malthus, *Essay on the Principle of Population*, 1798): population tends to increase in a **geometric progression** (1, 2, 4, 8, 16...) while the food supply increases only in an **arithmetic progression** (1, 2, 3, 4, 5...), because land is fixed and subject to diminishing returns. Population will therefore outrun food supply and be checked by **positive checks** (famine, disease, war) or **preventive checks** (moral restraint, late marriage). The view is **pessimistic**: **food supply limits population**.

**Boserup theory** (Ester Boserup, *The Conditions of Agricultural Growth*, 1965): population growth is not a threat but a **stimulus**. Population pressure on land forces people to **innovate and intensify agriculture** (shorter fallow periods, irrigation, new tools and techniques), so food output rises to meet the growing demand. The view is **optimistic**: **population drives agricultural change** ("necessity is the mother of invention").

| | Malthus | Boserup |
|---|---|---|
| Direction of causation | Food supply determines population | Population pressure determines food production |
| Population growth | A problem leading to checks and misery | A stimulus to innovation and technical progress |
| Technology | Fixed or slow, diminishing returns | Adapts and improves under pressure |
| Outlook | Pessimistic | Optimistic |

questions.enonce_markdown: Apart from population size, list two other aspects of a population that can influence production. (4 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
Any two aspects, each with a short explanation (2 marks each):

1. **Age structure (age distribution).** The share of the population of working age determines the size of the labour force. A large share of children or old people means a high dependency ratio, lower savings and a smaller labour force; a large working-age group raises potential output.
2. **Quality of the labour force (education, skills and health).** A healthy, educated and well-trained population is more productive, adopts new technology and is more entrepreneurial, so the same number of workers produces more.

Other acceptable aspects: **occupational distribution** (the share of workers in agriculture, industry and services), **geographical distribution and mobility** (rural-urban distribution, ability to move to where labour is needed), and **sex distribution and participation rate** (the proportion of men and women who take part in the labour force).
